Today we are splitting ⁦Ghostty's⁩ core into a library. The app you run keeps its window, its fonts and its configuration; the terminal underneath becomes something another program can embed.
A host hands libghostty a native surface and a size, and gets back a grid of cells it can draw however it likes. Input arrives as an event queue, not as callbacks into the ⁦host's⁩ event loop.
What does: everything that used to assume it owned a window.
An event queue instead of callbacks is the whole design in one sentence.
The ABI is versioned by struct size, so an embedder built against an older header keeps working until it asks for a field that did not exist yet.
The article describes Libghostty and its design.
libghostty splits Ghostty's core out of the app so another frontend can embed the terminal without the macOS shell. [1] [2]
The ABI is deliberately narrow: a surface, a grid of cells and an input queue, with no windowing or font policy in the library. [3]
Commenters split on whether a stable C ABI is worth the loss of Zig's comptime ergonomics inside the core. [4] [5]
The interesting part is what they left out. No windowing, no font stack, no config language — those all stay in the app. That is the whole reason this can be embedded.

The windowing split is the part I keep coming back to. Every terminal library I have tried eventually grows its own opinion about how a window should look, and then you are fighting it instead of using it.
Does the host get to choose the font, or does the library still own the cell grid? That is the line I keep tripping over when I try to imagine embedding this in a browser.
The library owns the grid; the host owns the surface. Fonts are the host's, which is why the cell metrics come in through the surface rather than through the config.
The design notes are worth reading for the input section alone. An event queue instead of callbacks is the whole design in one sentence.
The interesting question is what happens to the app's own escape-sequence handling once the library owns the parser. Two parsers in one process is a bad time.
I have wanted this for years. Every terminal library I have tried eventually grows its own opinion about how a window should look.
A narrow ABI is great until you need one more callback. Then you version the struct and every embedder has to care.
There is only one parser; the app talks to the surface, not to the wire.
Which is also why the input queue is an event queue and not callbacks. Callbacks would put the app back on the parser's stack.
Does the host get to choose the font, or does the library still own the cell grid? That is the line I keep tripping over when I try to imagine embedding this in a browser.
Related from 2024: the original libghostty design notes. The section on input is the one worth reading first.
